column3: Near-verbatim parallel: do not weaken while being the higher party; divine presence and unreduced deeds reinforce 3:139.
A secondary instance of granted distinction among believers, but not the communal endurance addressed in 3:139.
Names the aftermath directly: injury did not produce weakening, frailty, or surrender; patience holds the line.
Pairs the ban on grief with constriction caused by opponents' plotting, clarifying grief as a pressure to resist.
The conditional faith wording is shared, but the setting of an extraordinary birth adds little to 3:139.
Provides the contrary distribution: God weakens hostile scheming, whereas 3:139 forbids believers' weakening.
Faith grounds a moral warning here; the shared condition alone contributes little to steadfastness or grief.
The auxiliary work-and-compensation resonance is too remote from 3:139's exhortation.
Shows weakening as bodily depletion, a useful contrast to the commanded refusal of communal weakening.
Directly prohibits weakening amid mutual pain and sets believers' hope in God against the opposing side.
The shared faith condition is incidental to the birth narrative.
Contrasts reliable divine allegiance with a chosen protective structure that proves unable to bear weight.
Its faith-conditioned statement of what is better offers only a general ethical parallel.
The remote channel resonance does not clarify the command against weakness or grief.
Uses repeated weakness for embodied dependence, distinguishing that condition from the resolve commanded in 3:139.
Faith functions as a condition for a dietary command, not as the source of 3:139's confidence.
The nearby opposition context may explain pressure on the community, but it does not develop the exhortation itself.
Links steadfast confession with the explicit assurance not to fear or grieve, strongly echoing 3:139's faith condition.
The auxiliary crew-and-wage resonance is unrelated to the ayah's resilience theme.
The immediate Uhud aftermath names accumulated distress and the aim that believers not grieve over loss or injury.
Nearby defeat of opponents supplies campaign context but adds little beyond the surrounding sequence.
A brief posture term has no clear explanatory connection beyond a semantic retrieval match.
The auxiliary resonance is remote; its prayer for fellow believers does not explain 3:139.
Its statement about lack of faith is only a loose contrast to 3:139's conditional faith.
The local promise that endured migration, harm, fighting, and death are not lost supports confidence after setback.
Faith is tied to just communal repair; this offers a broad ethical frame, not a direct reading of being 'higher'.
The auxiliary work-recompense connection is not a substantive lens on 3:139.
The nearby confrontation with death exposes the test behind a command not to weaken after battle.
The shared local setting and channel label do not yield a focused addition to 3:139.
The phrase 'while you are' occurs in ritual regulation, with no meaningful link to the exhortation.
The auxiliary crew-and-wage resonance is too distant from the focus.
Personal grief and fear over a son's departure are a distinct situation from 3:139's communal command.
The record-and-recompense channel is auxiliary and does not explain perseverance or grief here.
Explicitly joins 'do not grieve,' divine companionship, support, and the lowering of the opposing word against God's highest word.
The remote labor-channel resonance does not add a supported reading of 3:139.
Depicts Pharaoh as arrogantly high, a contrary and corrupt form of elevation rather than 3:139's believing status.
The auxiliary channel is about a required offering and is not germane to the focus.
Describes a high garden, not the ethical or communal 'higher' status of 3:139.
The channel resonance supplies no direct semantic contribution to 3:139.
Physical elevation of Idris is distinct from the plural, faith-conditioned claim in 3:139.
The auxiliary channel does not provide an evidenced connection to the focus.
Directly counters fear of hostile allies and makes faith the condition for fearing God instead.
The remote wage-channel resonance does not illuminate 3:139.
Explicitly prohibits grief over opponents while directing a humble, protective posture toward believers.
The auxiliary channel does not yield a focused relation to 3:139.
Faith is presented as answering a summons under an existing covenant, supporting 3:139's conditional address to believers.
The labor-channel resonance is too indirect to be useful here.
Combines patience, the ban on grief, and resistance to constriction from opponents' plotting.
Frames costly struggle under a binding divine promise, supporting resolve after loss without duplicating 3:139.
A faith-conditioned legal command offers only a formal parallel.
The remote channel resonance does not clarify the focus.
Identifies internal dispute as causing failure and loss of collective force, then commands patience with divine presence.
Confronts fear of hostile opponents and redirects fear to God under the condition of faith.
The closing command of the same surah intensifies endurance, mutual endurance, vigilance, and God-consciousness.
Offers a concrete confidence formula: enter decisively, expect prevailing, and rely on God if believers.
Commands firmness when meeting an opposing force and abundant remembrance as the path to success.
Warns against relying on mocking opponents as protectors; this supports guarded communal allegiance.
Repairs relations and requires obedience in a conflict setting, identifying cohesion as a condition of resilient faith.
Its faith condition checks a request in a different setting and adds little to 3:139.
Exposes a claimed faith contradicted by rejection; it is a secondary contrast to 3:139's genuine faith condition.
A challenge about restoring life has no focused relation to the exhortation.
Links a sign of legitimate leadership with tranquility from God, a useful support for confidence under pressure.
The explicit assurance not to fear or grieve is joined to promised rescue, closely paralleling 3:139.
'Take with strength' supplies a contrary example of disobedient hearing, sharpening the demand for faithful resolve.
Requires verification and forbids denying another's profession of peace during movement in God's way; a restraint on conflict response.
A warning about raising voices concerns reverence and unnoticed loss of deeds, not 3:139's elevation.
Contrasts fear of false associates with accountable fear before God, reinforcing the reordering of fear in 3:139.
Its faith condition confirms signs in a different narrative and provides little beyond local surah context.
Assures the believing reformers that they will neither fear nor grieve; it supplies the same assurance in a broader horizon.
The incidental 'while you are' construction in fasting regulation has no semantic value for 3:139.
Promises that the greatest terror will not grieve its recipients, extending grief's removal to ultimate deliverance.
Associates belief and righteous action with reward and the removal of fear and grief; broadly corroborative but repetitive.
God's highest likeness is a theological use of 'highest,' distinct from the community's status in 3:139.
Shows disciplined vigilance and organized worship under danger, a practical pattern for refusing demoralization.
Repeats the no-fear/no-grief assurance with little new detail after the earlier parallel.
Defines the believing group by continued God-consciousness, adding a compact qualification to 3:139's faith condition.
Repeats reward and no grief for faithful good works; supportive but redundant with closer parallels.
The statement about disputed reality does not illuminate 3:139.
Identifies secret counsel as a means to cause believers grief, limits its harm by God's permission, and commands trust.
The brief phrase has no discernible connection to the focus.
A denial of faith without the relevant context adds no value.
Uses grief as Pharaoh's household's intended outcome, but it is not an exhortation or assurance to believers.
'Highest degrees' is an eschatological rank, not the communal superiority under pressure in 3:139.
God's being high and great is theologically distinct from the addressed believers being higher.
Domestic contentment and absence of grief are too remote from 3:139.
The rhetorical question about unbelief does not add a focused reading.
The ban on being grieved by those rushing into disbelief is relevant in wording but is addressed to the messenger in a different role.
The nearby exposure of those whose speech and hearts diverge clarifies why the faith condition cannot be merely verbal.
Sets fearful believers against Pharaoh's arrogant elevation, a contrary scene that distinguishes true faith from worldly dominance.
Uses divine highness in a domestic legal context; it does not clarify 3:139.
Guidance and good news for believers offer a general, redundant encouragement.
A specific prohibition with threatened punishment has no focused relation to the exhortation.
The absence of an intimate friend offers no explanatory link to 3:139.
The faith condition appears in fasting regulation, not communal resilience.
The dismay of disbelievers at an approaching reality does not clarify 3:139.
Condemnation for fabrication and arrogance does not add a focused relation.
An introductory statement about what they say has no usable connection.
Inheritance apportionment and the conditional wording are unrelated to 3:139.
Moses' collapse before divine manifestation and subsequent belief offer only a distant contrast to commanded steadfastness.
The report of weeping in a deceptive family episode adds no supported value to 3:139.
A direct counterpoint to fear: Moses is assured that he is the higher one, making this an essential omitted parallel.
Names two groups on the verge of losing courage and grounds their recovery in God's guardianship.
The immediate Uhud account explicitly identifies loss of courage, dispute, and disobedience as the path from initial success to reversal.
States the practical ground of being higher: with God's aid none can overcome, and without it none can help; believers rely on Him.
Reports a threat that increased believers in faith and moved them to a sufficiency-in-God response rather than collapse.
Shows the outcome of that response: return with favor and no harm after following divine good pleasure.
Directly addresses opponent hostility and makes patience and God-consciousness the defense against their plotting.
Frames injury as shared between sides and the alternation of days, supplying the historical logic behind refusing weakness after loss.
Joins forgiveness, firmness of feet, and help against opponents in the prayer of those who did not weaken.
Identifies God as believers' protector and the best helper, supplying the basis for confidence in 3:139.
Places tranquility after grief in the same Uhud sequence while exposing those consumed by self-concern.
In direct confrontation, believers seek poured-out patience, firm feet, and help against the opposing people.
Makes divine help both glad tidings and tranquility for hearts, an explicit remedy for demoralization.
Pairs strengthening believers with casting terror into opponents, closely matching the contrary resilience pattern.
Describes tranquility sent upon the messenger and believers at Hunayn when numbers had not sufficed.
The sight of the confederates increases believers in faith and submission rather than weakening them.
Promises that those who support God's cause will receive support and firm footing, directly developing steadfastness.
Defines tranquility as entering believers' hearts so that faith increases upon faith.
The upright believers receive the explicit assurance that they need not fear or grieve, an especially close omitted parallel.
Promises angelic reinforcement when the believers seek aid, supplying battle-context support for confidence.
Makes patience and God-consciousness conditions for further reinforcement in the same battle setting.
Warns believers that obeying disbelievers would turn them back as losers, a contrary path to remaining higher.
Locates the opponents' fear in divine action, reversing the community's temptation to be afraid.
Treats the setback as a moment of slipping under pressure and records divine pardon, complementing the recovery in 3:139.
Foretells hurtful opposition and calls patience and God-consciousness a matter requiring resolve.
Commands believers to seek help through patience and prayer and declares God's companionship with the patient.
Recalls severe shaking before divine help, giving a broad precedent for endurance under trial.
States that a small group can overcome a larger one by God's permission and that God is with the patient.
Attributes victory to God's permission after a disadvantaged force faces another, reinforcing non-material grounds of confidence.
Records believers seeking their Lord's aid and receiving promised reinforcement.
Describes security descending as sleep and purification before the encounter, a concrete relief of fear.
Calls believers to steadfast combat despite numerical disadvantage and ties endurance to divine knowledge.
Acknowledges weakness while promising that a patient group may overcome a larger one by God's permission.
Fixes reliance on God amid harm and benefit, guarding against the grief and weakening of adverse outcomes.
Recasts the opponents' waiting as a choice between two good outcomes for believers, resisting demoralization.
Makes trust in God the believers' response under tyrannical pressure.
Forbids despair of God's relief, supplying a broader prohibition against the hopelessness behind grief.
Promises God's companionship to the God-conscious and excellent, supporting the faith-conditioned assurance.
Affirms that God surely aids those who aid His cause, grounding confidence beyond apparent power.
Joins 'do not fear or grieve' to a divine promise of return and mission, a personal but direct verbal parallel.
Promises strengthened support and authority against hostile pursuit, a narrative instance of divinely secured standing.
Makes support for believers a divine commitment, supporting the declaration that they are higher.
Recalls the confederate threat and divine forces sent against it, giving the siege context for steadfastness.
Depicts the extremity of fear and shaken assumptions, clarifying the trial that 3:139 answers.
Names the believers' testing and severe shaking, a broad parallel to post-defeat pressure.
Honors believers who proved true to their covenant through death, waiting, and unchanged commitment.
Reports God repelling the hostile force without believers needing battle, leaving the opponents frustrated.
Promises help to messengers and believers in worldly life and at testimony, expanding the assurance of divine support.
Links divine pleasure, knowledge of hearts, tranquility, and an imminent victory for those who pledged commitment.
Contrasts hostile zeal with tranquility and the word of God placed upon the messenger and believers.
States the divine decree that God and His messengers will prevail, a theological basis for confidence without duplicating 3:139.
Promises believers divine help and a near victory, supplying an explicit horizon of encouragement.
The departure to assign believers positions for battle supplies nearby setting but adds less than the later direct verses.
Recalls aid at Badr despite apparent weakness, a useful but more distant precedent.
Describes purification of believers and erasure of disbelievers through the alternation of trial, only indirectly related.
Frames the ordeal as distinguishing those who strive and endure, a broad background to the exhortation.
The prayer for poured-out patience and faithful death supports endurance but lacks the focus's grief or elevation language.
The command to be patient and promise that good-doers' reward is not lost offer general support.
Messengers model reliance on God in the face of rejection, a secondary parallel.
The assurance of divine presence removes fear in a prophetic encounter, but not the communal status of 3:139.
Rewards patience after ridicule, offering a general end-state rather than the immediate battle exhortation.
The declaration of divine companionship at danger is supportive but narrative-specific.
The testing of claimed faith provides a general frame for the conditional faith in 3:139.
The promise of unmeasured reward for the patient supports endurance but is not a direct parallel.
